# Categories Enter through a Design Matrix

A categorical predictor records membership in a finite set of levels: treatment
arm, genotype, tissue, sequencing batch, or disease subtype. Regression software
cannot estimate a separate unconstrained coefficient for every level together
with an intercept, because the level indicators sum to the intercept. It therefore
represents a factor with $K$ levels using $K-1$ independent columns.

For a one-factor conditional-mean model,

$$
Y_i=\mu_{g(i)}+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{E}(\varepsilon_i\mid g(i))=0,
$$

the scientifically meaningful parameters are the level means
$\boldsymbol\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_K)^\mathsf{T}$. A coding scheme chooses a
full-rank coordinate system for the same $K$ means. Changing coordinates changes
the displayed coefficients, but not fitted values or any estimable comparison
computed consistently from the model.

This distinction is central:

- **Coding coefficients** describe a parameterization.
- **A contrast** describes a scientific comparison.
- **An estimate** is the contrast evaluated from the fitted model.

# Treatment Coding and Its Interpretation

With three levels—control, drug A, and drug B—and control as the reference,
treatment coding gives

$$
\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid g_i)
=\beta_0+\beta_A I(g_i=A)+\beta_B I(g_i=B).
$$

The coefficients are

$$
\beta_0=\mu_C,
\qquad
\beta_A=\mu_A-\mu_C,
\qquad
\beta_B=\mu_B-\mu_C.
$$

Thus the intercept is the control mean and each slope is a difference from
control. Changing the reference level changes all three coefficient meanings,
but the fitted group means remain $(\hat\mu_C,\hat\mu_A,\hat\mu_B)$.

Reference coding is convenient when one level is a genuine scientific baseline.
It is less useful when the questions concern a dose trend, an average of several
controls, or A versus B. Those questions should be stated as contrasts rather
than inferred indirectly from whichever coefficients software happens to print.

# A Contrast Is the Estimand

A linear contrast of level means is

$$
\psi=\mathbf c^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\mu
=\sum_{k=1}^{K}c_k\mu_k,
\qquad
\sum_{k=1}^{K}c_k=0.
$$

The zero-sum condition makes the comparison invariant to adding the same
constant to every level. Examples for $(C,A,B)$ include

| Question | Contrast weights $\mathbf c$ | Estimand |
|---|---:|---|
| A versus control | $(-1,1,0)$ | $\mu_A-\mu_C$ |
| B versus control | $(-1,0,1)$ | $\mu_B-\mu_C$ |
| A versus B | $(0,1,-1)$ | $\mu_A-\mu_B$ |
| Average drug versus control | $(-1,1/2,1/2)$ | $(\mu_A+\mu_B)/2-\mu_C$ |

Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ be the fitted coefficient vector with covariance
$\widehat{\mathbf V}$. If the desired comparison is
$\psi=\mathbf l^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\beta$, then

$$
\hat\psi=\mathbf l^\mathsf{T}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta},
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\psi)
=\sqrt{\mathbf l^\mathsf{T}\widehat{\mathbf V}\mathbf l}.
$$

An interval or test follows from this estimate and standard error using a
reference distribution appropriate to the design and covariance estimator. The
contrast should be chosen because it answers a prespecified question, not because
it produces the smallest p-value.

# Other Coding Systems

Different full-rank codings emphasize different coordinates:

| Coding | Typical coefficient interpretation | Important caution |
|---|---|---|
| Treatment/reference | Each nonreference level minus a baseline | Intercept and slopes depend on the chosen reference |
| Sum-to-zero | Deviations from an equally weighted grand mean | The grand mean is not the sample-size-weighted mean in an unbalanced design |
| Helmert | A level compared with an average of subsequent or previous levels | Direction and scaling conventions differ among software |
| Polynomial | Linear, quadratic, and higher-order patterns across ordered levels | Meaningful only when ordering and spacing are defensible |
| Custom | Coordinates aligned with planned scientific hypotheses | Must have adequate rank and documented weights |

Orthogonal contrast vectors satisfy $\mathbf c_j^\mathsf{T}\mathbf c_k=0$ for
$j\ne k$. In a balanced one-way design, their sums of squares partition the
factor sum of squares. In unbalanced or covariate-adjusted data, algebraic
orthogonality of the weights does not necessarily imply uncorrelated estimates.

A factor with $K$ levels contributes $K-1$ degrees of freedom. A single
coefficient test answers one coordinate-specific question; an omnibus
$K-1$ degree-of-freedom test asks whether all relevant level differences are
zero. A nonsignificant omnibus test does not validate every equality, and a
significant omnibus test does not identify which contrast matters.

# Adjustment Changes What Is Being Compared

With additional covariates,

$$
\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid g_i,\mathbf z_i)
=\alpha+\text{factor terms}(g_i)+\mathbf z_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol\gamma,
$$

factor coefficients are conditional comparisons at the same $\mathbf z$. If
there are no factor-by-covariate interactions, the adjusted difference is
constant over $\mathbf z$. With interactions, there is no single group
difference until values or a distribution of $\mathbf z$ are specified.

Estimated marginal means compute model-based predictions for each level and
average them over a declared reference distribution of covariates. Equal
weighting across cells, weighting by the observed sample, and weighting by a
target population answer different questions. In unbalanced observational data,
calling one of them “the adjusted mean” without stating the averaging rule hides
part of the estimand.

Adjusted comparisons also require overlap. If a treatment occurs only in one
batch, the treatment and batch columns are aliased: no coding scheme can recover
their separate effects. Sparse treatment-by-tissue cells may technically permit
a fit while making the requested contrast largely extrapolative.

# Worked Example: Three Library-preparation Methods

Suppose RNA integrity is measured for independent donor samples processed by a
standard method $S$ or alternatives $A$ and $B$. The fitted adjusted means are

$$
(\hat\mu_S,\hat\mu_A,\hat\mu_B)=(7.10,7.45,7.20).
$$

The planned contrast comparing the average alternative with the standard method
is

$$
\hat\psi
=-\hat\mu_S+\tfrac12\hat\mu_A+\tfrac12\hat\mu_B
=0.225.
$$

That estimate does not equal the A-versus-S coefficient, the B-versus-S
coefficient, or an unweighted average of all three means. Its standard error
must use the covariance among the three fitted means; treating their individual
standard errors as independent is generally wrong.

If the same donor material was split across methods, donor is a blocking or
repeated-measures unit and the model must retain that pairing. If different donors
received different methods, donors are the independent experimental units.
Technical lanes, aliquots, and reads do not increase the biological replication
unless the target explicitly concerns technical repeatability.

# Diagnostics, Sensitivity, and Reporting

Before interpreting a factor or contrast:

1. **Verify levels and reference meaning.** Check spelling, unused levels,
   ordering, and whether a numeric code was accidentally treated as continuous.
2. **Inspect the design matrix.** Confirm rank, columns, aliases, empty cells,
   and the coding actually used by the software.
3. **Inspect cell counts and overlap.** Report independent units per relevant
   factor combination, not only the total record count.
4. **Check the outcome model.** Residual, variance, dependence, and influence
   diagnostics still apply; factor coding does not repair misspecification.
5. **Define the contrast family.** Prespecify the comparisons and use simultaneous
   intervals or multiplicity adjustment when many claims form one family.
6. **Test coding invariance.** Refit with another full-rank coding and confirm
   that fitted values and explicitly reconstructed contrasts agree.
7. **State the averaging population.** For marginal means, document covariate
   values and weights.

Report the contrast weights or plain-language comparison, estimate, uncertainty
interval, scale and units, covariance method, adjustment set, and multiplicity
procedure. A coefficient table alone is not a complete account of a multi-level
factor.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Multiple linear regression](multiple-linear-regression.qmd) defines the
  design-matrix model in which factor columns are fitted.
- [Least squares and the geometry of regression](least-squares-and-regression-geometry.qmd)
  explains rank, estimability, and covariance of linear functions.
- [Regression uncertainty and coefficient interpretation](regression-uncertainty-and-coefficient-interpretation.qmd)
  develops conditional coefficients, contrasts, and prediction uncertainty.
- [Interaction terms and effect modification](interaction-terms-and-effect-modification.qmd)
  shows why a factor effect can depend on another predictor.
- [Bonferroni, Holm, and Hochberg procedures](../statistical-inference/bonferroni-holm-and-hochberg-procedures.qmd)
  addresses multiplicity across planned or exploratory contrasts.

1. A coding scheme parameterizes group means; a contrast defines the scientific
   comparison.
2. Full-rank recoding changes coefficient labels, not fitted values or consistently
   computed estimable contrasts.
3. In unbalanced data, adjusted or marginal means depend on an explicit covariate
   distribution and weighting rule.
4. Empty cells, aliasing, and poor overlap are design problems that recoding
   cannot solve.
5. Biological inference follows the number and structure of independent samples,
   not the number of technical observations.
